Paper_name: Happy me: Asymmetric bidirectional links between the self and positivity underpin biased processing
Summary: Three experiments combined evaluative priming with shape-label matching to examine the mechanisms and directionality of self-valence links. In Experiment 1a, happy (vs. neutral) emotional primes preceding personal shape-label matching (self/friend/stranger) enhanced the self-stranger RT bias by inhibiting stranger-related targets rather than facilitating self-related targets. Experiment 1b applied the same logic with sad (vs. neutral) primes and found no prime effects on self-bias magnitudes. Experiment 2 reversed the priming direction: personal identity primes (participant's own first name = self; stranger's name = stranger) preceded emotional shape-label matching (happy/neutral/sad), and self-primes enlarged the positivity bias by facilitating happy targets rather than inhibiting sad targets. Results reveal an asymmetric bidirectional self-positivity link whose dominant mechanism (inhibition of distal others vs. facilitation of positive content) depends on priming direction; negative valence produced no analogous effects at the level of perceptual matching.
Author: Naomi A. Lee, Douglas Martin, Jie Sui
Conclusion: Self and positivity are linked not by a single mechanism but by two direction-dependent mechanisms: when emotional information precedes self-other judgements, positive primes enhance self-biases through inhibition of socially distant (stranger) targets; when self-relevant information precedes emotional judgements, self-primes enhance the positivity bias through facilitation of congruent positive targets. Negative valence does not reciprocate this relationship at the level of perceptual matching. The findings extend self-enhancement theory and predictive-processing/reward accounts of self-concept maintenance.
